citation.title: A Supervised Machine Learning Approach for Accelerating the Design of Particulate Composites: Application to Thermal Conductivity
citation.authors: Mohammad Saber Hashemi, Masoud Safdari, Azadeh Sheidaei

claim.primary_outcome_paraphrase: A learned conductivity surrogate is used inside inverse design to reduce the cost of evaluating candidate particulate microstructures relative to direct packing and FFT homogenization.
claim.claimed_speedup_basis: Section 3.2 reports about 0.1 seconds for surrogate prediction versus an average 1+3 hours per microstructure for packing plus homogenization; using 4 hours / 0.1 seconds gives approximately 144,000× (derived from rounded values).
claim.alternatives: Section 3.3 reports an average one-minute inverse-design optimization and verifies one selected conductivity prediction with FFT.

baseline.classical_method: Genetic algorithm using direct microstructure packing and FFT homogenization for objective evaluations
baseline.implementation: Elitist GA; Rocpack dense packing and in-house FFT homogenization
baseline.solver: FFT homogenization; optimizer is genetic algorithm
baseline.hardware_classical: AMD Ryzen 1950x CPU, 32 GB DDR4 RAM (Section 1)
baseline.hardware_ml: AMD Ryzen 1950x CPU, 32 GB DDR4 RAM (Section 1)
baseline.problem_size: Particulate composite RVE; microstructure descriptors include particle volume fraction, aspect ratio and size distribution (Section 2.1, Table 1)
baseline.classical_time: Packing average 60 min/RVE plus FFT homogenization 180 min/RVE (Table 4)
baseline.ml_time: About 0.1 s per surrogate prediction (Section 3.2); inverse design average 1 min (Section 3.3)
baseline.training_time: 1 min reported for surrogate training and prediction/RVE in Table 4
baseline.data_generation_cost: Packing 60 min/RVE and FFT homogenization 180 min/RVE (Table 4); dataset uses almost 10,000 Sobol points (Section 3.1)
baseline.quality_metric: Thermal conductivity from FFT homogenization; target conductivity and surrogate error
baseline.quality_gap: For the inverse-design example, target 3 W/mK, surrogate prediction 2.9 and FFT result 2.7 W/mK (Section 3.3).

R1.evidence: Sections 3.2–3.3: computational advantage is reported without a matched-time or matched-quality comparison against a classical optimization result.

R2.evidence: Sections 2–3: no protocol criterion establishing an inefficient classical solver or hardware mismatch was found.

R3.evidence: Sections 2.1 and 3.2–3.3, Table 4: data generation and model costs are described, but break-even use count is not given.

R4.evidence: Section 3.3: the selected design is checked by FFT homogenization, but infeasible or failed design rates are not reported.

reporting.n_test_cases: One detailed inverse-design case (target 3 W/mK) in Section 3.3; validation/test samples also reported in Section 2.2.

notes: Source: arXiv full text. Data supplementary to the article are linked through the stated project repository; no public runnable code was established.
